mcq.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) primarily resolves names to IP addresses, e.g. example.com to an A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) record.
mcq.distractors: Building binaries, scheduling containers and encrypting disks are unrelated to name resolution.

mcq.explanation: An IP address identifies a network interface on an IP network; a host with several NICs (or IPv4 and IPv6) has several addresses.
mcq.distractors: Image tags, CPU instructions and Git repositories have their own identifiers that have nothing to do with IP.

mcq.explanation: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery using a handshake, sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission.
mcq.distractors: UDP is connectionless with no delivery or ordering guarantee, ICMP carries control messages like ping, and ARP maps IPs to MAC addresses.

mcq.explanation: `ping` sends ICMP echo requests and reports replies and round-trip time, testing basic reachability.
mcq.distractors: `git status`, `chmod` and `docker build` do not touch the network in this way. Note some hosts block ICMP, so no reply does not always mean down.

mcq.explanation: HTTP 404 means resource not found: the server is reachable and answered, but there is nothing at that path.
mcq.distractors: Success is 200, authentication problems are 401/403, and no HTTP status means 'server started'.

mcq.explanation: HTTPS defaults to port 443 (HTTP over TLS).
mcq.distractors: 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS and 80 is plain HTTP.

mcq.explanation: `curl` makes HTTP (and many other protocol) requests from the terminal, e.g. `curl -I https://example.com`.
mcq.distractors: `tar` archives files, `mkdir` creates directories and `grep` searches text.

mcq.explanation: A subnet mask or prefix (e.g. /24 = 255.255.255.0) indicates the network portion of an IP address; the remaining bits identify hosts.
mcq.distractors: It has nothing to do with volumes, passwords or DNS TTLs.

mcq.explanation: The default gateway forwards traffic to other networks: any destination not on a local subnet is sent to it (the default route).
mcq.distractors: Compiling, starting services and resolving merge conflicts are not routing functions.

mcq.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell, TCP port 22) gives encrypted remote shell access.
mcq.distractors: DHCP assigns addresses, FTP transfers files (unencrypted by default) and SMTP sends mail.

labs.modelAnswer:
# 1. IP address and subnet
ip -br addr        # or: ip addr show
# eth0  UP  192.168.1.25/24
# Interpretation: interface eth0 has IP 192.168.1.25; /24 is the prefix, i.e. subnet mask 255.255.255.0, so the local network is 192.168.1.0/24 (hosts .1-.254).

# 2. Default route
ip route
# default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
# 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.25
# Interpretation: traffic to other networks goes to gateway 192.168.1.1 via eth0; the second line means the local subnet is reached directly.

# 3. Listening ports
sudo ss -tulnp
# tcp LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22   users:(("sshd",...))
# tcp LISTEN 0 511 127.0.0.1:80 users:(("nginx",...))
# Interpretation: sshd accepts connections on port 22 from any address; nginx listens on port 80 but only on localhost, so it is not reachable from other machines.
labs.explanation: Tests reading a Linux host's network configuration with the modern iproute2 tools (`ip addr`, `ip route`, `ss`). The interpretation matters as much as the command: identify the interface IP, convert the prefix to a subnet, name the gateway from the `default via` line, and note which address each listening socket is bound to (0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1).

labs.modelAnswer:
Target: web service on 10.0.0.5:80

# Step 1 - reachability
ping -c 4 10.0.0.5
# 100% packet loss / 'Destination Host Unreachable' => reachability problem (host down, routing, firewall dropping ICMP). Check ip route and security groups.

# Step 2 - is the port open? (on the server)
sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':80'
# no output => nothing listening: closed port (service stopped or bound to another port)
# from the client:
curl -v http://10.0.0.5/
# 'Connection refused' => host reachable but port closed => systemctl status nginx, start it
# 'Connection timed out' => a firewall is likely dropping packets to the port

# Step 3 - HTTP response
curl -i http://10.0.0.5/health
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK => healthy
# HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found => wrong path; 502/503 => proxy up but backend app failing; check app logs
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://10.0.0.5/

Conclusion: ping fails => reachability; ping OK but 'connection refused' and ss shows no listener => closed port; TCP connects but status is 4xx/5xx => HTTP/application issue.
labs.explanation: Tests layered troubleshooting: network layer (ping), transport layer (is a socket listening, does TCP connect) and application layer (HTTP status). Look for the decision logic: which symptom from each tool points to which cause. Remember ICMP may be blocked, so a failed ping with a working curl is not a contradiction.

checks.label: Records the DNS result (IP / A record)

labs.modelAnswer:
# DNS
dig example.com +short
# 93.184.215.14   (example output; your result may differ)
nslookup example.com
# Name: example.com  Address: 93.184.215.14
# DNS result: example.com has an A record pointing to 93.184.215.14

# HTTP
curl -sI http://example.com
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://example.com

# HTTPS
curl -sI https://example.com
# HTTP/2 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'status %{http_code}\n' https://example.com
# status 200

# Record: DNS -> 93.184.215.14; HTTP status 200; HTTPS status 200 (TLS handshake OK). A 301 on HTTP would mean a redirect to HTTPS; follow it with curl -L.
labs.explanation: Tests the end-to-end path of a web request: name resolution, then HTTP and HTTPS over TCP. Check that the answer records the actual IP returned and the status code for both schemes, and explains anything unusual (e.g. 301/308 redirects from HTTP to HTTPS, or TLS certificate errors). `dig +short` and `curl -w '%{http_code}'` give clean, scriptable output.
